reader: AI reader 35 (targeted check at the stated place)
sources_read: Nutt & de Wit 2021, Madero & Alvarez 2023, Earleywine et al. 2025, Marseille & Mitchell 2025 and Mahase 2024 from the project PDFs (pdftotext -layout, every page rendered at 110 dpi, Tables 1 and 2 of Earleywine checked on the rendered pages). The three retraction notes (10.1007/s00213-024-06666-x, -06665-y, -06671-0) read in full on link.springer.com in my own browser tab (tab-10, opened and closed by me), with the Crossref records of each note and each retracted article; for cross-checks only, the MAPP1 abstract and author information on nature.com and the Crossref records of MAPP1, MAPP2 and Nutt & de Wit's references 8 and 10, in the same tab, and the Crossref record of their reference 4 in a second tab of my own (tab-8, opened and closed by me). No PDF link was opened and nothing was downloaded.

results.note: Earleywine p. 2, Introduction 3rd paragraph (left column, the first paragraph on the page): rejection cited to Marks 2024 (JAMA); 'a split vote' of an independent advisory committee with no counts; concerns about maintaining the blind given MDMA's psychoactive effects, the sufficiency of long-term safety data and therapist behaviour (Jacobs 2024; Jarow 2024a, 2024b), disentangling MDMA from the psychotherapy, and generalizability given homogeneous samples (Jarow 2024b). No vote count anywhere in the paper. Role qualifies: right for the blinding claim (a second-hand report of the committee's concern).

Read both pages (standfirst, 11 running-text paragraphs, Fig. 1 legend, 12 references, competing interests) and searched the text: blinding, placebo, expectancy, the comparison condition, the sample size and every trial number are absent; the only controlled study mentioned is a healthy-volunteer one (refs 8, 9). 'Significant efficacy and an excellent safety profile' is in the 1st paragraph (p. 950, middle column). Role qualifies: right.

corrected.extracted: Describes the first phase 3 trial (Mitchell et al., 2021) as randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled and multi-site, with a significant attenuation in CAPS-5 score compared with placebo and as much as two thirds of the MDMA arm no longer meeting PTSD criteria after completing treatment (no count, week or placebo-arm figure; 'after completing treatment' points to completers); then says the safety profile appears favourable because MDMA did not induce adverse events of abuse potential, suicidality or QT prolongation, in a sentence with no citation of its own that follows the one citing the trial. Nothing is said about whether the blind held or about expectancy.

results.note: Page and locator right: p. 19, 3rd paragraph (it begins at the foot of the left column; the content is in the right column). Two fixes to the extracted text. (1) The source does give a time reference, after completing treatment, which also implies the completers as denominator, so 'no time point' overstates the gap; what is missing is the count, the week and the placebo-arm figure. 'Two thirds' agrees with the completers' 28 of 42 (67%) that cl_mdma_ptsd_efficacy carries. (2) 'Without a citation' is literally true of the sentence, but it follows the sentence citing Mitchell et al. (2021) and repeats almost word for word the MAPP1 abstract's own statement on abuse potential, suicidality and QT prolongation (abstract read on the publisher's page for this check); the issue is repetition of the trial's summary without appraisal, not an unsourced claim. Role qualifies: right.

p. 20, Declaration of Competing Interest (right column): O.A. is a principal investigator for the phase IIB and III clinical trials in the MAPS-sponsored MDMA-AT trials for PTSD and reports no other conflicts; S.M. reports none. Role qualifies: right.

p. 20, 6th paragraph: it begins at the foot of the left column (phase 2 and 3 findings 'might revolutionize' treatment, Gonda et al.; Solmi et al.) and the hype-bubble (Yaden et al., 2022) and lowered-standards (Hall and Humphreys, 2022) sentences open the right column, followed by the warning that the combination might prove disastrous without the highest ethical and scientific standards. Neither point is applied to the trials described. Wording nit only: the source speaks of debate over the lowering of standards by major journals publishing psychedelic trials. Role qualifies: right.

p. 950: the standfirst says only that MDMA may be a promising treatment; significant efficacy, an excellent safety profile in people with severe PTSD and the forecast of approval in a few years are in the 1st paragraph's continuation in the middle column. No trial number anywhere (both pages checked). Role qualifies: right.

p. 951, 10th paragraph (right column): the new evidence is said to support efficacy and safety after just a few exposures at what the authors call a relatively moderate dose, without signs of tolerance or dependence; no data. Role qualifies: right.

results.note: Same anchor text and same two fixes as n = 29 (time reference given; the safety sentence repeats the MAPP1 abstract's own wording and follows the citation of the trial). For this claim the point matters more: 'did not induce adverse events of ... suicidality' means no excess over placebo, not none, since the MAPP1 anchors in this same claim record suicidality events of special interest in 3 of 46 on MDMA (against 5 of 44). Role qualifies: right.

p. 20, 5th paragraph (left column): inherent risks, introduced as for almost any effective approved treatment; risks increase in recreational settings (abuse potential, triggering of psychiatric disorders, especially with pre-existing vulnerabilities such as psychotic disorders); after approval, administration limited to certified centres with defined safety screenings and a centralized pharmacy; trained therapists under supervision. Role qualifies: right.

As n = 27 (p. 2, Introduction 3rd paragraph, left column; every concern listed is there, with the news and JAMA sources). Role qualifies: right for the adverse-event claim (long-term safety data, therapist behaviour).

p. 6, Discussion 4th paragraph (the one beginning 'Based on these new data', right column): no citation for the FDA statement; the next sentence cites Penn and Yehuda (2023) and Zamaria et al. (2025) for knowledge gaps, not for the FDA. Quotation verbatim, 10 words. Role qualifies: right.

p. 1, 2nd paragraph under 'FDA rejects Lykos Therapeutics' application' (left column): minutes of the 4 June advisory committee meeting show that the majority of experts did not believe the data showed the drug was effective in patients with PTSD and that all but one said its benefits did not outweigh its risks; ref 7 is the final summary minutes dated 30 July 2024. No counts. Role qualifies: right.

corrected.extracted: The notices did not detail the violations; reports (ref 4, a New York Times article of 12 August 2024; ref 5, a 2019 MAPS statement announcing an ethical violation by former MAPS-sponsored investigators) suggest that a trial investigator at one study site had an unethical sexual relationship with a trial participant; in a 2018 lawsuit settled out of court the participant said she had been sexually assaulted, and the investigator said it was consensual (ref 6, a CBC report).

results.note: Page and locator right (p. 1, 3rd paragraph of the opening section, left column). One fix: refs 4 and 5 are not both press reports. The article says only 'reports suggest'; ref 4 is the New York Times and ref 5 is the sponsor's own 2019 public statement (its URL is dated 24 May 2019). Ref 6, cited for the lawsuit, is a CBC report of March 2022 whose title names a trial in British Columbia. Role qualifies, but this claim's statement does not use the anchor (see my claims file).

Notice read on link.springer.com: published 10 August 2024 (vol. 241, p. 2405; issue November 2024); the header gives the original's publication date as 7 May 2019 and cites it as (2019) 236:2735-2745. Both paragraphs as extracted: MP4 site, authors' later confirmation, no disclosure or removal of the site's data, competing interest not fully declared (several authors with MAPS or MAPS PBC); responses: Feduccia agrees but not with the wording, six disagree, Walsh neither, the remaining two (Hamilton, Emerson) did not respond. The notice's sentence that MAPS 'fully funded and provided the MDMA' is ambiguous about what was funded; the anchor's reading (MAPS funded the work) is fair. Crossref update-to and updated-by links agree. Role qualifies, but this claim's statement does not use the anchor.

p. 1, 1st paragraph under the subheading (left column): the retractions came after the FDA rejected Lykos' new drug application for MDMA capsules for PTSD. No date for the decision anywhere in the article (published 13 August 2024). Role supports: right.

p. 1, Introduction, 1st paragraph: Stanicic et al. (2024), funded by Lykos, came after the FDA declined to approve in August 2024 (McPhillips, 2024: a CNN report, accessed 27 November 2024 per the reference list); the abstract speaks of the FDA's 2024 decision to decline approval. Role supports: right; the month rests on this second-hand source alone.

results.note: Same fix as n = 54: the article says 'reports suggest', and ref 5 is the sponsor's own 2019 statement, not a press report. The claim's statement repeats 'press reports' and should change with the anchor. Role qualifies: right.

p. 1, last paragraph of the right column (7th under the subheading): 'Reports show' that the research in the three retracted papers did not form part of the application; no reference number. Role qualifies: right.

p. 1, Inappropriate choice of comparator, 1st paragraph (left column, ending at the top of the right column with SSRIs such as sertraline or paroxetine and the trial's three 8-hour sessions with two clinicians): identical therapy with placebo; appropriate for regulatory approval but not actionable for payers. Role supports: right.

p. 1, 2nd paragraph of that section (right column): head-to-head data lacking; the authors' prior analyses (Marseille et al., 2020, 2022) modelled standard care; base case with no new costs or changes in health status for the comparator; 11,537 against 48,376 dollars, the latter as cited in Stanicic et al., driven primarily by the drug cost; net savings at the five-year horizon. Which of the two earlier analyses gave 11,537 is not said ('our study'). Role supports: right.

The 2nd paragraph ends at the top of p. 2, left column: about 84,000 dollars per QALY for MDMA versus placebo-therapy, technically under a 150,000-dollar threshold but not especially compelling to payers. Role supports: right.

p. 2, Methodological strengths despite flawed comparator, 1st paragraph (trial-derived outcomes and PTSD-care use; 17-month follow-up from MAPP2 and MPLONG) and 2nd paragraph (documented reduction in health-care use; only PTSD-specific costs, broader costs of comorbidities excluded). No numbers. Role supports: right.

p. 2, Drug pricing, 1st paragraph (12,000 dollars per dose, three dosing sessions, 36,000 for the regimen, therapy excluded; break-even 3.8 years in their 2022 analysis at a much lower price, about 8.4 years with 36,000, beyond the average enrolment of most US plans) and 2nd paragraph (10,500 dollars for three doses gives 160 dollars per QALY over five years; dominant below 10,320). No inputs or ranges anywhere in the paper. Role supports: right.
p. 3, Conflict of interest and source of funding (right column): consulting fees (Marseille) and research support (Mitchell) from MAPS PBC/Lykos; no funding for the study. Role qualifies: right.

p. 20, 5th paragraph, last sentence (left column): access for 25-75% of eligible patients with chronic and severe PTSD over 10 years; 43,000 to 106,000 deaths averted; 3.3-8.2 million QALYs; 109 to 266 billion dollars in net savings for the US healthcare system (Avanceña et al., 2022, whose authors include Marseille in the reference list). Madero calls it a cost-effectiveness analysis; its title calls it a modelling study. Role supports: right.

Content right: p. 1, Introduction 2nd paragraph (begins in the left column; d = 0.91 and 0.70 in the right column); the reference list on p. 9 gives MAPP1 as 27(5):720-28 with Doblin third and MAPP2 as 29(9):2020-29 with double-blind in its title, against Crossref's 27(6):1025-1033 (Doblin 38th of 38) and 29(10):2473-2480 (a randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial), which I checked. Role: this is the yes side of the debate, a second-hand restatement of the trial results; in this claim the trials' own results (anchors 0 and 1) carry 'qualifies', and a second-hand account of them cannot support the insufficient-evidence statement more than the trials do.

Content right: p. 7, Discussion 9th paragraph (right column): MAPP2 included a more diverse group and reported significant reductions in PTSD (Mitchell et al., 2023), which the authors call a cause for optimism, adding that only new data can support generalization. Role as for n = 87.
